n: This is the turning point of the Flood story: “God remembered Noah.” In scripture, God’s remembering means He acts on His promises. A wind blows over the waters, echoing the Spirit moving over the waters at creation.

f.g: To “remember” in Hebrew means to act faithfully for someone, not just to recall.
Hebrew ruaḥ — wind, breath, or spirit; the same word as in Genesis 1:2.
Subsided; went down.

n: The sources of the flood are shut off above and below. The chaos is brought back under God’s control.

f.g: Held back.

n: Slowly the waters recede. After 150 days they have noticeably gone down.

f.g: Decreased; lessened.

n: The ark comes to rest in the mountains of Ararat, a region in modern eastern Turkey and Armenia. The word “rested” echoes Noah’s name, which means rest.

f.g: The ancient land of Urartu, around eastern Turkey and Armenia—a region, not necessarily the single peak known today as Mount Ararat.
Hebrew nuaḥ, the root of Noah’s name.

n: Months pass before mountaintops appear. Noah’s faith requires long patience.

f.g: About two and a half months after the ark grounded.

n: After forty more days Noah opens the window. He is cautious and patient, testing before acting.
Noah sends a raven, which flies back and forth. Ravens eat carrion and can survive outside, so it does not return with useful news.

f.g: Back and forth.

n: Next Noah sends a dove—a gentle bird that needs dry land and plants. Doves become a symbol of peace and of the Holy Ghost.
The dove finds nowhere to land and returns. Noah tenderly reaches out and draws her back into the ark—a small picture of God gathering in the weary.

f.w: no rest for the sole of her foot

n: Noah waits seven more days, then sends the dove again. Hope and patience go together.

f.g: Waited.

n: The dove returns with a freshly plucked olive leaf—proof that trees are growing again. The olive leaf has become a lasting symbol of peace and new life.

f.g: Joseph Smith called D&C 88 “the olive leaf … plucked from the Tree of Paradise, the Lord’s message of peace to us.”
Freshly picked—not floating debris.

n: After another week, the dove does not return; she has found a home. The earth is ready for life again.

f.w: returned not again unto him any more
f.g: The dove’s absence is good news.

n: On New Year’s Day of Noah’s 601st year, the ground is dry. Noah removes the covering and sees a new world. A new year, a new beginning.

f.w: the first month, the first day of the month
f.g: The earth’s renewal falls on a New Year’s Day.
The roof or cover of the ark.

n: Almost two months later the earth is fully dry. Noah and his family had been in the ark about a year in all.

f.g: Counting from 7:11, about a year and ten days.

n: Noah waited for God’s word before leaving the ark, just as he had waited before entering it. God now speaks.

f.g: Noah did not leave on his own judgment, even though the ground was dry.

n: God tells the whole family to go out. As at entering, so at leaving: they move at God’s command.
The animals are to go out and multiply. God renews the creation blessing of Genesis 1—this is a fresh start for the earth.
Noah and his family step out into the cleansed earth.

f.g: Noah again obeys immediately.

n: Every creature leaves by families, in order, after their kinds.

f.g: Literally “by their families”—an orderly exodus.

n: Noah’s first act is worship. He builds an altar—the first one named in the Bible—and offers sacrifices of clean animals in gratitude. Sacrifice pointed forward to Jesus Christ.

f.g: Offerings wholly burned on the altar, symbolizing total dedication to God.

n: The Lord accepts the offering and resolves never again to curse the ground or destroy all life this way, though human hearts are still prone to evil. God’s mercy, not human goodness, guarantees the future.

f.g: A pleasing aroma—a way of saying God accepted the offering.

n: God promises that the seasons and the cycle of day and night will continue as long as the earth lasts. Every sunrise and harvest is a reminder of His faithfulness.
